# Pharmacologic interrogation of USP28 cellular function in p53 signaling

**Authors:** Ariana S. Bratt; Susan Kilgas; Maria I. Tarazona Guzman; Robert S. Magin; Isabella Jaen Maisonet; Cara A. Starnbach; Wei Pin Teh; Anthony C. ## Abstract

Deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs) are crucial regulators of ubiquitin signaling and protein degradation that remain incompletely understood in part due to the lack of high quality chemical probes. To address this challenge, we developed CAS-010, a low nanomolar, ubiquitin-competitive inhibitor of USP28 that demonstrates preferential activity against USP28 over other DUBs, while also exhibiting some activity against the closely related USP25. We rationalized our SAR trends and observed selectivity using a crystal structure of USP28 in complex with an inhibitor. We validated on-target effects of CAS-010 on the p53 pathway in the p53 wild-type setting. We demonstrated that CAS-010 disrupts the 53BP1-USP28 interaction, and more broadly showed that USP28 catalytic activity contributes to this key interaction. Taken together, CAS-010 and the accompanying negative control compound WPT-086 and inhibitor-resistant mutant provide well-validated tools for further characterizing the role of USP28 in p53-mediated effect on cell cycle control and cell fate.

## Introduction

Deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs) are isopeptidases that regulate ubiquitin signaling by cleaving ubiquitin from protein substrates or editing ubiquitin chains1. DUBs are therefore an important factor in the wide range of cellular processes involving ubiquitination, such as protein homeostasis, cell signaling, cell cycle control, DNA damage repair and autophagy2,3. DUBs have been implicated in a range of immunological, neurodegenerative and neoplastic diseases, and represent an emerging drug target class4–10. Their translational potential has recently been demonstrated by the entry of drug candidates targeting USP1 (Clinical Trial IDs NCT05240898 and NCT06331559) and USP3011,12 into clinical investigation. Notably, a USP30 inhibitor MTX652 that regulates mitophagy has been approved for Phase 2 study for protection against acute kidney injury in high-risk cardiac surgery patients11. Despite this progress, the physiologic roles of the majority of DUBs have not been well characterized, leaving the therapeutic potential of the DUB family largely untapped.

USP28 is a DUB whose biological functions remain incompletely characterized. Studies suggest that USP28 plays diametrically opposite functions of a tumor suppressor regulating wild-type (WT) p53 via 53BP1-dependent and -independent mechanisms13–19 and an oncogenic protein through stabilization of oncogenic transcription factors including c-Myc20, c-Jun21, Notch121, LSD122, and ∆Np6323. Further genetic studies suggest that USP28’s role in stability of these oncogenic factors may be heavily expression and tissue-dependent24. Despite USP28’s critical role in regulating p53 activation, mice deficient in USP28 exhibit minimal phenotypic changes, maintaining a normal lifespan and typical radiation responses25–28. These findings suggest that USP28’s function may be more nuanced and context-dependent than previously recognized. Therefore, temporally controlled depletion or inhibition of USP28 is crucial to fully unravel its role in cell cycle regulation and proliferation, as well as to explore the therapeutic potential of USP28-targeting drugs.

High-quality chemical probes can be invaluable tools to efficiently assess DUB function across multiple contexts by creating specific, acute loss of function, and could provide further insight into USP28 biology to augment our understanding of its physiological roles29. Low potency, early generation inhibitors AZ130 and Vismodegib31, and a more potent, recently reported inhibitor FT20632 have been shown to decrease levels of c-Myc in certain contexts. However, how USP28 inhibitors affect p53 signaling has not been examined.

To further investigate USP28 biology, we conducted an extensive SAR campaign using a lead small molecule we previously identified in a screen as a dual USP28/25 inhibitor33, and ultimately developed and characterized CAS-010, a potent (IC50USP28-FL = 2.2 nM) and selective USP28 inhibitor, as well as the negative control compound WPT-086. Like previously reported USP28 inhibitors, CAS-010 also exhibits activity against the closely related DUB USP25, although our studies demonstrate preferential inhibition of USP28. We obtained a high-resolution crystal structure of USP28 in complex with a compound in the series, which lead to mutant studies, identifying genetic tools for further study of USP28 function. We demonstrate that with respect to viability, CAS-010 phenocopies the genetic KOs of USP28 and p53-related genes. We show that CAS-010 reduces p53-mediated gene transactivation and disrupts the 53BP1-USP28 complex, which is known to be essential for p53 transactivation functions17. Importantly, we use genetic tools in corroborating experiments to both confirm on-target USP28 effect and provide additional insight into the mechanism of 53BP1-USP28 interaction. Our findings establish CAS-010/WPT-086 and the engineered USP28 mutants as valuable chemical biology tools to further investigation USP28 function in this signaling pathway.

## Results

### Development of a USP28 inhibitor CAS-010

We recently described discovery and characterization of the dual USP25/28 inhibitor, Bin-01-07-07 (Figure 1A)33. Although potent in biochemical assays (USP28 catalytic domain IC50 = 120 nM) and selective for USP25/28, Bin-01-07-07 did not engage USP25/28 in live cells, and exhibited poor metabolic stability. Therefore, Bin-01-07-07 was not suitable as a chemical tool compound for cell-based and pharmacological studies. Thus, we initiated a medicinal chemistry campaign to develop a chemical probe for USP28 using Bin-01-07-07 as a starting point, focusing on improving potency and metabolic stability while maintaining selectivity. For the purposes of structure-activity relationship (SAR) investigations, we dissected the molecule into four regions for optimization: the 3,4-dimethoxyphenethylamine attached to the pyrimidine, the aromatic core, and the propyl and cyclopentane groups appended to the thienopyrimidine. We generated a wide range of derivatives that were profiled in a biochemical assay using recombinant USP28 catalytic domain and the fluorogenic DUB substrate ubiquitin-rhodamine (UbRho) to identify compounds with improved potency.

The majority of changes resulted in either no change or decreased potency (Table S1). Nevertheless, opening of the pyrimidine ring, which generated Bin-01-68, improved inhibition compared to Bin-01-07-07 by 2-fold in recombinant USP28 (IC50 = 50 nM; Figure 1B). In addition, we confirmed compound binding and selectivity against native enzymes DUBs in HEK293T cellular lysates using competitive activity-based protein profiling (ABPP) coupled with quantitative mass spectrometry34. The ABPP-MS assay measures the ability of compounds to block labeling of DUBs by ubiquitin-containing activity-based probes (ABPs), which label the catalytic cysteine residue of DUBs. Inhibition of DUB catalytic function results in decreased labeling by the ABP. In this assay, compared to Bin-01-07-07, Bin-01-68 demonstrated improved blockage of activity-based probe binding of native USP25 and USP28 and maintained selectivity for USP25/28 over 58 other endogenous DUBs (Figure S1A). Therefore, we used Bin-01-68 to generate the next series of inhibitors (Figure 1C, Table S2). Removal of the cyclopentyl group resulted in Bin-01-78, a single-digit nM inhibitor (IC50 = 8.7 nM; Figure 1C). Bin-01-78 labeled native USP25/28 in cell lysates and retained selectivity for USP25/28 (Figure S1A). Unfortunately, Bin-01-78 did not exhibit engagement of USP25/28 in live cells as determined by the same competitive ABPP assay resolved by western blot (Figure S1B), or improved microsomal stability compared to Bin-01-07-07 (Table S3).

Given these outstanding liabilities despite improvements in potency, we revisited the 3,4 dimethoxyphenyl group, removing the methoxy groups and introducing a piperazine at the 4-position of the aromatic ring, changes aimed to improve microsome stability35 and cellular permeability36, respectively. This inhibitor, MTG-01-99 (Figure 1D), maintained potency similar to Bin-01-78, maintained selectivity for USP25/28 (Figure S1A) and, importantly, engaged the targets in cells (Figure S1B). We further replaced the piperazine with different rings, with piperidine (CAS-13312-011) and morpholine (MTG-03-162) containing compounds showing the strongest inhibition while maintaining relative selectivity for USP25/28 (Figures 1D and S1A). While working on this project, a core scaffold similar to Bin-01-68 appeared in the patent literature37. We synthesized SB1-B-55 (henceforth referred to as B55; Figure 1E), a compound inspired by one of the most potent analogs in the patent. B55 demonstrated strong inhibition of USP28 (IC50 = 65 nM) and selectivity for USP25/28 (Figure S1A). B55 showed promising microsomal stability (Table S3) and in-cell target engagement (Figure S1C). This motivated us to combine our improved core scaffold with the 4-substituted saturated heterocycle feature in B55 resulting in CAS-13312-010 (referred to as CAS-010; Figure 1F). CAS-010 was the most potent compound in this series (IC50 = 4.2 nM) (Figure 1D). Importantly, initial target engagement studies showed the compound exhibited the most potent cellular target engagement of any compound tested (Figure S1C) and promising microsomal stability (Table S3). We synthesized and validated a negative control compound WPT-086 (IC50 > 10 μM; Figure 1G), which we designed based on our SAR studies in which installation of a dimethylamide group to the pyridine ring substantially reduced potency (Figure 1C). We carried CAS-010 and WPT-086 forward for further in-depth validation and characterization.

### CAS-010 is a potent and selective inhibitor of USP28

To further validate CAS-010 and WPT-086 as a USP28 chemical probe/negative control compound pair for cell-based and pharmacological interrogation, we performed additional biochemical experiments. We validated that CAS-010 also inhibits recombinant full-length USP28 with single-digit nanomolar potency (IC50 = 2.2 nM) (Figure 2A). We tested whether CAS-010 inhibits the activity of the closely related USP25 consistent with other USP28 inhibitors30–32, and determined that it has more than 10-fold lower potency compared to USP28 (USP25 catalytic domain IC50 = 75 nM; USP25 full length IC50 = 51 nM) (Figure 2B). Since USP25 has the capacity to form an autoinhibited tetramer, to ensure that autoinhibition of USP25 was not confounding the apparent potency of CAS-010 against USP25, we also compared USP28 to the USP25 mutant P521A, a point-mutation which prevents the tetramerization39. We found that CAS-010 is less potent against this USP25 construct compared to USP28 (USP25 P521A IC50 = 57 nM) (Figure 2B). A kinetic experiment with UbRho as a substrate indicates that CAS-010 is a competitive inhibitor of ubiquitin binding in USP28 (Figure S2A).

We evaluated compound activity against a panel of purified DUBs using Ubiquigent’s DUBProfiler™. At a compound concentration of 10 μM, CAS-010 demonstrates strong inhibition of and exquisite selectivity for USP25/28 compared to 28 other USPs, while WPT-086 exhibits no USP25/28 activity (Figure 2C). In an ABPP-MS experiment in HCT116 lysate, CAS-010 blocked labeling of USP28 and USP25 by the ABP in a dose-dependent manner, while not binding the other 57 DUBs detected in this experiment (Figure 2D, left). In this experiment, USP28 was labeled substantially more potently than USP25, consistent with what was reported for the structurally similar FT20632. The negative control WPT-086 did not affect ABP labeling of USP28, or any other DUB, at concentrations as high as 25 μM (Figure 2D, right). Using the same competitive ABPP assay with live cell treatment and western blot analysis, we confirmed that CAS-010 precludes ABP binding to USP28 at nanomolar concentrations in a dose-dependent manner, supporting that CAS-010 is able to bind USP28 in cells (Figure 2E; note that in the case of USP25, presence of autoinhibited tetramers interferes with probe binding and this assay cannot report on USP25 accurately).

Lastly, we also demonstrated that CAS-010 is suitable for in vivo studies, with a half-life of 81 minutes in mice and an oral bioavailability of 37% (Figure S2B). In both IV and oral dosing of mice, plasma concentrations of CAS-010 exceeded concentrations at which CAS-010 engages USP28 in cells (Figure S2C).

To ensure the robustness of our characterization, we evaluated CAS-010 against community-endorsed criteria for chemical probes40. CAS-010 meets benchmarks for biochemical and cellular potency, selectivity and inclusion of a negative control, which together with its favorable pharmacokinetic properties, support both its utility as a chemical probe and its translational potential41 .

### Structural analysis reveals mechanistic insights into USP28 inhibition by CAS-010 inhibitor series

To better understand molecular determinants that govern USP28/CAS-010 binding, we attempted co-crystallization of the catalytic domain of USP28 (amino acid 149-703, with 399-580 domain replaced with GSGSGS to facilitate crystallization, as reported before39) with multiple potent compounds from our medicinal chemistry efforts. B55 (Figure 1E) yielded high-quality crystals, which diffracted to 1.96 Å resolution (PDB: 7TUO; Figure 3A, Figure S3A, Table S4). The structure revealed that B55 binds at the interface of the palm, finger, and thumb sub-domains of USP28, occupying a pocket located about 10 Å from the catalytic cysteine. Notably, B55 extends into the ubiquitin-tail-binding channel (PDB: 6HEI), engaging a surface pocket that overlaps with the binding site for Leu73 of the ubiquitin C-terminus (Figures 3B and 3C), thereby sterically blocking ubiquitin binding. These structural insights align with our biochemical evidence from Michaelis-Menten kinetic analysis of competitive inhibition by this compound series (Figure S2A).

Beyond direct competition at the ubiquitin binding channel, structural data reveal conformational changes in key structural elements and residues. Comparison of apo-USP28 (PDB: 6HEH) and Ub-bound USP28 (PDB: 6HEI) structures demonstrates a shift in the α5 helix into an active conformation, which aligns residues in the “switching loop”, (a well-studied regulatory feature immediately preceding the α5 helix39,42–45) with the C-terminus of the ubiquitin (Figure S3B). In our inhibitor-bound USP28 structure, the α5 helix is shifted relative to that in apo-USP28, apparently to accommodate compound binding, although there is no obvious steric interference between the compound and the globular core of ubiquitin (Figure 3D). This shift disrupts ordering of the switching loop, which becomes unresolved in electron density maps, indicating it is highly disordered and unable to effectively coordinate the C-terminus of the ubiquitin (Figure 3E).

In addition to shifts in the α5 helix, the phenyl-8-azabicyclo[3.2.1]octane ring of B55 locks Phe370, Tyr601 and Tyr643 into positions comparable to apo-USP28, preventing them from adopting the “open” conformation seen with Ub-bound USP28 (Figure 3F). These aromatic residues are highly conserved across the USP family and their movement is understood to be critical to forming a channel through which the C-terminal tail of ubiquitin can thread for cleavage46. Together, these structural features support a model in which CAS-010 and its analogs inhibit USP28 by occupying the Leu73-interacting pocket and stabilizing an inactive conformation of USP28 that is not compatible with ubiquitin binding and cleavage.

The binding region of B55 overlaps with multiple previously reported regulatory or inhibitor-binding regions. It partially overlaps with the ‘distal’ binding pocket previously described for the USP7 inhibitor, GNE6776 (PDB: 5UQX)42 (Figure S3C) and the ubiquitin-tail-binding channel targeted by other USP7 inhibitors47,48 (Figure S3D). Notably, binding site of B55 also overlaps with that of the auto-inhibitory motif of USP25 (PBD: 6HEL)39 (Figure S3E). Additionally, concurrent with the preparation of this manuscript, structures of USP28 bound to different inhibitors were reported, including AZ1 (PDB: 8P1P) and Vismodegib (PDB: 8P14), and FT206 (PDB: 8P1Q), the latter of which shares the same core as B55 and CAS-01038. Each inhibitor occupies the same pocket, engaging in different areas within pocket. Our USP28-B55 structure reveals closer similarity with each of the USP28-inhibitor bound structures compared to both apo- and Ub-bound USP28 structures (PDB: 6HEH and PDB: 6HEI respectively) (Table S5). Structural alignment showed that B55 and FT206 display almost perfect alignment of their shared aromatic cores and similarly extend into the ubiquitin-tail-binding channel, sterically overlapping the region that accommodates Leu73 and thereby occluding ubiquitin binding (Figure S3F). In contrast, AZ1 engages more deeply within the allosteric pocket and does not sterically compete with ubiquitin (Figure S3G), consistent with reported kinetic studies supporting a non-competitive mechanism of inhibition30. Comparison to recently published USP28-inhibitor structures further supports the B55 binding mode observed in our structure, and highlights how distinct chemical scaffolds can engage the same regularly pocket to elicit different inhibitory mechanisms.

### USP28-inhibitor interactions define determinants of binding affinity and selectivity

A survey of the ligand binding site revealed multiple critical interactions between B55 and USP28 involving: (1) Hydrogen bonds between (a) a pyrazine nitrogen and Gln315 and (b) the amide nitrogen and Glu366 (Figure 4A); (2) multiple contacts between the thienopyrazine core and Val176, Leu180, Thr260, His261, Leu264, Met288, Phe292, Leu590, Cys644 and Met646 (Figure 4B); and (3) interactions of the phenyl ring and 8-azabicyclo[3.2.1]octane rings and Val256, Ser257, Phe370, Lys381, His592, Ala596, Tyr601 and Tyr643 (Figure 4C). Lastly, two well-ordered, ligand-buried water molecules form hydrogen bonds with the amide oxygen, Thr260, and Tyr643, as well as with each other (Figure 4A).

To examine the importance of these residues for compound binding, we generated a series of USP28 mutants with single amino acid substitutions. Thr260, Gln315, and Glu366, as well as additional residues around the binding pocket (Val176, Leu180, His261, Phe292, Tyr293, Thr364, Leu590, and Tyr643) were mutated to alanine, and Cys644 was mutated to leucine or methionine.

All USP28 mutants retained the ability to cleave ubiquitin at single-digit nanomolar enzyme concentrations, with the exception of Tyr293Ala and Tyr643Ala which significantly showed reduced catalytic activity (Figure S4A). We found that mutants His261Ala, Glu366Ala, Cys644Met and Cys644Leu were more active compared to wild-type, His590Ala was similarly active compared to wild-type, while the remaining mutants were somewhat less active than the wild-type. Patzke et al similarly found USP28 mutants His261Ala and Glu366Ala to be hyperactive38. B55 inhibited most of the mutants but with reduced potency (Figures 4D and S4B, Table S6). Interestingly, the Glu366Ala mutant was resistant to B55, indicating that the hydrogen bond between B55 and Glu366 is a key determinant of binding. Additionally, Thr260Ala and His261Ala also exhibited significantly weaker potency, thus highlighting the importance of these two residues for compound binding. To validate that CAS-010 binding is consistent with our USP28-B55 co-crystal structure, we tested CAS-010 against Glu366Ala and Thr260Ala USP28 mutants and observed significantly weaker potency in these mutants compared to wild-type USP28 (Figure 4E), indicating that USP28-B55 structure accurately captured interactions relevant to CAS-010 binding.

In order to rationalize the specificity of our inhibitor for USP28 and USP25 over other DUBs, we performed and examined the sequence alignment of the USP domains49 of all USPs (Figure S4C). The sequence alignment revealed multiple residues that are unique to USP28 and USP25, such as Cys644 (USP28 numbering), and Thr260 positioned across the pocket from Cys644. In other DUBs, these residues are bulkier, with Leu, Met, Ile, Val, or His found in position homologous to Cys644, and Leu, Met, Phe, or Tyr typically found instead of Thr260 (Figure 4B). Based on our structure of USP28-B55 complex, the two residues are close to the ligand; therefore, having larger residues at these positions likely sterically interferes with the ligand binding. Additionally, Gln315 and Glu366, which are directly involved in ligand binding, are nearly unique (Gln315) or entirely unique (Glu366) to USP28 and USP25, with other USPs featuring aspartic acid and a histidine or glutamine, respectively (Figure 4A). Taken together, our structural analysis provides a framework for understanding the key determinants of tight binding between the CAS-010 series of inhibitors, and coupled with the sequence alignment, enables us to map likely features that explain the observed selectivity.

### Integration of structural, SAR and mutational data reinforces principles of USP28 inhibition

The crystal structure corroborates principal SAR-derived insights and validates that compound binding in solution is consistent with the structure. For example, varying the chain off the thienopyrimidine altered potency, with propyl > methyl > pentyl > H >> aromatic (Table S2). In our structure, the methyl on the analogous thienopyrazine of B55 is positioned in a hydrophobic pocket and has a van der Waals interaction with Phe292 (Figure 4B). B55 exhibits a 3-4-fold loss of potency against USP28 Phe292Ala, supporting that this interaction contributes to potency, consistent with our SAR. Based on the structure, extending the chain to a propyl would put the chain in closer proximity to Phe292 strengthening this interaction, while a pentyl would sterically clash.

Removing the cyclopentyl ring in the adjacent position improved potency significantly, while increasing the bulk and/or hydrophilicity of the substituent substantially decreased potency (Figure 1C). This observation served as the basis of our negative control compound’s design with the hydrophilic, bulky dimethylamide substitution. These observations are rationalized with the crystal structure which would orient this group into the small, hydrophobic pocket in the structure defined by Leu180 and Leu264 (Figures 1C and 4B). B55 exhibits a 20-fold loss of potency against USP28 Leu180Ala. As our structure indicates that L180 would sterically clash with the dimethylamide of the negative control compound WPT-086 (Figure S4D), we tested WPT-086 against Leu180Ala as well as Leu180Val mutants. WPT-086 inhibits the alanine mutant with an IC50 of 27 μM, compared with wild-type USP28 in which the compound does not demonstrate 50% inhibition even at the highest concentration of 400 μM (Figure S4E). The compound binds slightly better to the valine mutant compared to the wild-type, in keeping with the affinity for the compound being increased with decreasing size of the USP28 residue. Replacement of Leu180 with the smaller alanine opens a space for this compound with its bulky side chain to bind with increased affinity. This finding identifies a bump-and-hole pair to optimize as another tool for elucidating USP28 biology50,51.

We determined the amine off of the pyrimidine in Bin-01-07-07 to be essential to maintaining potency, where derivatives with a methylamine (Bin-01-49) or an oxygen in place of the nitrogen (Bin-01-104), had a >1,000-fold loss of potency (Table S1). This supports the need for a hydrogen bond donating group at this position, which is consistent with the structure which places the amide in the analogous position on B55 to form a hydrogen bonding interaction with Glu366, and with the finding that B55 exhibits a substantial loss in potency when tested against the USP28 Glu366Ala. Patzke et al. explored the importance of Glu366’s hydrogen bond and negative charge in compound binding. Integrating our SAR data with mutant studies, we conclude, in agreement with their findings, that a hydrogen bond between the amide of our compound and Glu366 is one of the strongest drivers of potency in this compound series.

Opening the pyrimidine of Bin-01-07-07 to include an amide (Bin-01-68) improved potency (Figure 1B), which can be rationalized with the observation in the crystal structure that the carbonyl oxygen of the amide forms a hydrogen bond with a water molecule which also interacts with Thr260. The importance of this interaction is further validated with the Thr260Ala mutant which B55 inhibits far less potently than wild-type.

Finally, consistent with kinetic and structural evidence of competitive inhibition, the bulky 8-azobicyclic ring present in B55 and CAS-010 contributes to the superior potency of these compounds compared to close derivatives with different tail components (Figure 1D).

Collectively, our SAR, structural and mutational analyses converge to define molecular features governing USP28 inhibition, validating on-target compound engagement. With this mechanistic understanding established, we next explored the cellular phenotype of USP28 inhibition to gain insight into its biology.

### Effect of CAS-010 treatment on cancer cell viability mirrors USP28 knockout and correlates with knockout of TP53-related genes and intrinsic p53 activity

To define the phenotype of USP28 inhibition by CAS-010, we used the Broad Institute’s PRISM assay to profile the effects of CAS-010 on cell survival. In this assay, ~800 cancer cell lines were treated with CAS-010 in a dose-response, and cell viability was measured after five days52 (Figures S5A and S5B). We compared the viability phenotype of CAS-010, to the CRISPR knockout data set from the Cancer Dependency Map (DepMap), which includes 18,000 gene CRISPR knockouts across 1,100 cancer cell lines53. We focused on the cell lines present in both data sets, with the majority of correlations representing analysis from >660 cell lines. For each gene, we calculated the correlation between CAS-010-treated viability (log2-fold change) and gene knockout sensitivity (Chronos dependency score)54,55. The correlations are visualized in a volcano plot (Figures 5A–D), where each individual point represents an individual gene knockout and reflects the strength and statistical significance of its correlation with CAS-010 viability effects.

The viability profile of CAS-010 treated cells correlates strongly with USP28 knockout (KO) across a broad range of cell lines, meaning that CAS-010 closely phenocopies genetic loss of USP28, supporting on-target effect (Figures 5A–D). In contrast, there was no significant correlation with USP25 KO, underscoring that USP25 engagement is not a primary determinant of CAS-010’s effects on cell viability. Strikingly, CAS-010 was also strongly correlated with knockouts of p53 pathway genes, including 53BP1, TP53 and ATM, and negatively correlated with genes that suppress p53 activity, such as MDM256,57. Similarly, when USP28 knockout was compared to the knockout of other genes in the DepMap CRISPR KO data set, the strongest correlations (codependencies) were with p53-related genes (Figure 5E), consistent with previous reports demonstrating the relevance of USP28 in mediating p53 activation13–15,17,18. In contrast, the top USP25 KO gene codependencies (Figure 5F) did not overlap with those of USP28 KO, nor did they correlate with CAS-010 response. Interestingly, we did not identify a correlation between MYC (or other oncogenes) and USP28 modulation by inhibitor or knockout in these analyses.

To explore the relation with p53 further, we analyzed the viability phenotype of USP28 modulation by CAS-010 inhibition or genetic knockout in the context of p53 function using DepMap’s mutation and gene expression data sets. We found that the effect on viability depended on the cell’s TP53 mutational status (Figures S5C and S5D). Specifically, TP53 mutant cells show no significant change in viability, whereas TP53 wild-type cells exhibit relative increase in viability in response to USP28 inhibition or knockout. This suggests that TP53 wild-type cells may maintain or even enhance proliferation under USP28 perturbation, consistent with the known role of p53 in cell cycle regulation. Analysis of all hotspot mutations across cell lines confirmed that TP53 hotspot mutations negatively correlated with cell viability (Figures S5E and S5F). Additionally, viability effect in the setting of USP28 modulation correlated with the expression of p53 target genes (Figures S5G and S5H), which are more highly expressed in TP53 wild-type settings (Figure S5I). These findings provide evidence that USP28 modulation affects cells proportional to their p53 activity.

Taken together, these unbiased data and analyses reveal that CAS-010 inhibition of USP28 recapitulates the effects of USP28 genetic loss both with respect to viability and p53 relationship. Overall, this highlights USP28’s known strong functional link to p53 and p53-dependent pathways, and therefore we focused our attention to examining these relationships further.

### CAS-010 attenuates p53 gene transactivation

Based on our cancer cell line profiling data, we hypothesized that USP28 inhibition with CAS-010 would suppress p53 signaling and transactivation, consistent with genetic studies describing USP28’s role in p53-mediated gene transactivation13,15,17,18. To test this, we utilized a luciferase reporter system combined with Nutlin-3a (N3), a small molecule inhibitor of MDM2 that promotes p53 transactivation58. In a stable U2OS cell line expressing two p53 response elements (RE) under a luciferase reporter, treatment with CAS-010 caused a decrease in p53 activity compared to negative control WPT-086 in response to Nutlin-3a (Figure 6A).

We further determined the effect of USP28 inhibition on p53 signaling by assessing the transcription of p53 target genes. CAS-010 suppressed N3-induced expression of cell cycle regulators CDKN1A (p21) and MDM2, and the pro-apoptotic target BAX in both U2OS and RPE-1 cells compared to WPT-086 (Figures 6B and 6C). Importantly, in cells with USP28 knockdown (KD) by siRNA, CAS-010 had no effect on p53 target gene expression (Figures 6D and S6A). This provides strong evidence that CAS-010’s effect on the p53 transcriptional pathway is mediated through USP28 and not an off-target mechanism. Treatment with AZ1 and FT206 also reduced p53 gene target transcripts in RPE-1 and HCT116 cells (Figures S6B and S6C), supporting that modulation of these genes is a shared effect of USP28-targeting compounds.

Next, we assessed the effect of USP28 inhibition on p21 protein levels across several TP53 wild-type cell lines. CAS-010 treatment resulted in a dose-dependent decrease in p21 across all tested cell lines (Figure S6D). Conversely, we did not observe a decrease in c-Myc in the same conditions. To confirm that USP28 was effectively engaged, we performed a simultaneous target engagement assay in HCT116 cells and observed full USP28 inhibition with CAS-010 (Figure S6E). Under the same experimental conditions, treatment with AZ1 and FT206 led to decreased Myc levels, consistent with prior reports30,32. In the TP53 null CALU-1 lung squamous cell carcinoma line, CAS-010 treatment had no effect on p21 protein levels (Figure S6F), supporting that CAS-010’s effect on p53 target genes is p53-dependent. Additionally, in RPE-1 cells, CAS-010 reduced p21 and p53 protein levels both with and without ionizing radiation (IR), consistent with a DNA damage-independent effect on p53 signaling (Figure S6G).

### CAS-010 affects p53 gene transactivation by modulating 53BP1-USP28 interaction

Previous studies have established that 53BP1 serves as a scaffold for USP28 binding, which in turn promotes p53 binding and its subsequent transcriptional activation14,16,27. To examine whether CAS-010 affects the USP28-53BP1 interaction, we performed co-immunoprecipitation of endogenous 53BP1 in RPE-1 cells. As expected, USP28 co-precipitated, and CAS-010 treatment led to a reduction in USP28 levels in the 53BP1 pulldown, consistent with disruption of the USP28-53BP1 interaction (Figure 7A).

To examine this effect in situ, we employed a proximity ligation assay (PLA) in RPE-1 and U2OS cells, both with and without IR-induced DNA damage. CAS-010 treatment significantly decreased 53BP1-USP28 PLA foci in both cell lines and conditions (Figures 7B and S7A–D).

To evaluate whether the PLA results reflect on-target engagement of USP28 and assess the role of USP28 catalytic activity on the USP28-53BP1 interaction, we performed a PLA in RPE-1 USP28 KO cells transfected with either wild-type, catalytically inactive (Cys171Ala), or inhibitor-resistant (Glu366Ala) USP28. CAS-010 had no effect on PLA foci in cells expressing the inhibitor-resistant Glu366Ala mutant, supporting a direct, on-target mechanism (Figure 7C). In contrast, under negative control treatment, cells expressing the catalytically inactive Cya171Ala mutant exhibited significantly reduced PLA foci compared to wild-type USP28 cells, phenocopying the effect of CAS-010 in wild-type cells (Figure 7D). Moreover, CAS-010 had no additive effect in Cys171Ala-expressing cells, supporting that loss of catalytic activity is sufficient to diminish this interaction. Together, our results support a model in which catalytic inhibition of USP28 by CAS-010 decreases 53BP1-USP28 interaction.

## Discussion

DUBs represent an emerging class of drug targets, with several agents now progressing through clinical trials8,10. However, despite this rising interest and the deepening insight that DUBs regulate numerous homeostatic and pathogenic cellular processes, the family remains incompletely characterized. In general, availability of high-quality chemical probes can accelerate biological and pharmacological research, inspiring us to focus on providing quality tool compounds for the study of DUBs. For example, we previously developed and validated high-quality probes for USP748,59. We also identified inhibitors that can serve as starting points for chemical probe development using high-throughput screening methods33,34. This included Bin-01-07-07, which we use here as a starting point to develop CAS-010, a new chemical probe for USP28 that satisfies all community-endorsed standards40 as it: (1) inhibits USP28 with single digit nM IC50; (2) is highly selective, with additional inhibitory activity towards USP25 only, out of 72 DUBs evaluated across two orthogonal profiling assays; (3) binds endogenous USP28 in live cells in the 100 nM range as determined by competitive ABPP providing proof of in-cell target engagement; (4) has a negative control compound available and validated (WPT-086); (5) it does not affect USP28 KD and KO cells, indicating that its phenotypic effects are dependent on the presence of its target; and (6) it does not affect cells expressing inhibitor-resistant mutants, further validating on-target effects. Collectively, CAS-010 meets all the community criteria regarding chemical probe validation, and can be used to probe USP28 biology.

To understand molecular features that govern potency and selectivity, we solved a structure of USP28 catalytic domain bound to a compound from the CAS-010 series, B55. The enzymatic and structural data show that B55 competes directly with ubiquitin by blocking access the catalytic site. Additionally, compound binding induces conformational changes that further preclude ubiquitin coordination. We confirmed importance of key residues involved in the compound binding through site-directed mutagenesis. Moreover, we identified drivers of specificity by analyzing sequence alignments across the USP family of DUBs. We identified Glu366 and Gln315 as key determinants of USP25/28 specificity, which agree with recent findings of Patzke et al.38, as well as Thr260 and Cys644, which have not been reported before.

By integrating our high-resolution structural data with our extensive SAR and targeted mutagenesis, we generated a cohesive and mechanistically grounded model of USP28 inhibition. This multi-pronged approach complements and extends previous studies by directly linking compound features to potency, selectivity and functional outcomes across structural and biochemical contexts. Finally, we developed inhibitor-resistant mutants, as well as a candidate bump-hole pair, providing a platform for orthogonal chemical-genetic approaches. Such systems can be powerful in rescue experiments to validate on-target inhibitor effects60,61, and offer unique tools to dissect USP28-specific functions, especially valuable given the compound’s dual, albeit weaker, activity against USP25.

USP28 is a DUB reported to be involved in divergent biological processes, from stabilizing oncoproteins20–23 to promoting tumor suppressing activity of p5314,15,17,19. Therefore, inhibiting USP28 could have a wide range of functional outcomes, so we started with an unbiased strategy to profile our compound involving hundreds of cell lines (PRISM screen) and thousands of genes (DepMap). We discovered that cell viability effects of CAS-010 phenocopy genetic knockouts of USP28, TP53, 53BP1 and other p53-related genes. In addition to the correlation to USP28 KO which indicates on-target USP28 inhibitor effect, these results establish that the effect of CAS-010 on viability across the PRISM data set is p53 pathway-dependent. We observed no correlation between the PRISM and DepMap data sets to Myc or other oncogenes. In our very limited examination of Myc, we did not see changes in protein levels of Myc as has been reported with other inhibitors30,32. The lack of effect could well be explained by the context and dose dependence of USP28 modulation on Myc and other oncoproteins that has been described24.

Guided by our PRISM results, we focused our studies on USP28 inhibitor effect on p53 signaling. Our experiments represent the first reported pharmacologic studies demonstrating USP28-mediated p53 signaling, in which treatment with CAS-010 in multiple cell lines resulted in reduced levels of the p53 target transcripts CDKN1A, MDM2, and BAX. Importantly, the effects were rescued by USP28 knockdown, validating the CAS-010 effect as being the result of its USP28 binding. This corroborates genetic data and sets the stage for further mechanistic studies to elucidate USP28’s role in p53-mediated gene transcription.

Finally, we evaluated the effect of CAS-010 on USP28-53BP1 interaction using co-immunoprecipitation and proximal ligation assays. CAS-010 treatment decreased USP28-53BP1 interaction in USP28 wild-type cells, and studies using USP28 inhibitor-resistant and catalytic inactive mutants further demonstrated that the CAS-010 effect is directed by its inhibition of USP28, and more broadly that USP28 catalytic activity contributes to its interaction with 53BP1. While it has been demonstrated previously that USP28 catalytic activity is important for p53-dependent gene transactivation14,17, to our knowledge this is the first evidence that USP28 catalytic activity can influence USP28’s interaction with 53BP1. Taken together, our data supports a model whereby CAS-010 binds and inhibits USP28, which in turn affects 53BP1-USP28 interaction, and consequently p53-dependent gene transactivation. Further mechanistic studies will be important to understand how USP28 catalytic activity influences this interaction.

In conclusion, integrating our chemical probes and genetic tools, we have established a robust toolkit for probing USP28 function with precision in cellular contexts. Employing this set of chemical biology tools, we showed that CAS-010 reduces p53 gene transactivation and further present evidence that CAS-010 mechanisms of action include modulation of protein-protein interactions, providing new insight into the functional role of USP28 in the 53BP1-p53 axis.

### Significance

The DUBs are a family of isopeptidases which regulate ubiquitin signaling, therefore playing key roles across the spectrum of cellular functions. The functions of many DUBs, such as USP28, have yet to be fully explored and understood. No studies to date had used pharmacologic methods to interrogate USP28 function in an unbiased way, nor to characterize the effect of inhibiting USP28 on p53 signaling, a reported USP28 function. We sought to develop and validate a USP28 probe suitable for these studies.

Our extensive medicinal chemistry campaign resulted in a selective, single-digit nanomolar USP28 inhibitor. Similar to other USP28-targeting compounds, this inhibitor also binds the closely related USP25, albeit with lower potency. The compound is able to bind USP28 in live cells and has a favorable pharmacokinetic profile, therefore establishing our compound as a USP28 probe suitable for cell-based and in vivo studies. In addition, we developed a close derivative which lacks USP28 inhibitory activity to use as a negative control compound. This represents the first published USP28 inhibitor-negative control compound pair, an important tool for gaining confidence in on-target effects.

We present a USP28-inhibitor crystal structure which identifies an allosteric pocket in which the compound binds which prevents ubiquitin from reaching the DUB catalytic site. The structure corroborates SAR findings from our medical chemistry efforts. Based on our structure, we designed a dozen point mutants which we employed to validate the binding mode and identify key interactions to explain both potency and selectivity. The inhibitor-resistant mutants are additional tools for the study of USP28 function.

Cancer cell line screening with our inhibitor, analyzed along with DepMap data, provided strong evidence of our USP28 inhibitor effect on p53 signaling in TP53 WT cells. Focused follow-up experiments in cells confirmed USP28 inhibitor treatment decreases p53 activation. Finally, we showed that the USP28 inhibition disrupts 53BP1-USP28 interaction, which creates a novel hypothesis that USP28 catalytic activity contributes to this interaction.

#### Quantitative Activity-Based Protein Profiling

Cells (HEK293T for Figure S1A experiment, HCT116 for Figure 2E experiment) were lysed in 5 pellet volumes of lysis buffer (50 mM Tris pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, 0.5% NP-40, 10% glycerol containing protease and phosphatase inhibitors) and the lysate was clarified by centrifugation (16,000 x g for 10 minutes at 4°C). Each experimental condition (compound x concentration) was performed in duplicate. Treated lysates were then incubated with 75 nM of Biotin-Ub-PA and Biotin-Ub-VME mix (UbiQ) for 15 minutes at room temperature. Target enrichment was performed on a KingFisher APEX magnetic bead processor using 40 μL magnetic streptavidin bead slurry (CYTIVA) per well as follows: the beads were incubated with extracts for 30 minutes and washed in three consecutive 1-minute washes in PBS containing 0.2% SDS, water and ethanol (500 μL each). The beads were released and incubated in 50 μL of hexafluoro isopropanol (HFIP) for 5 minutes to elute the captured proteins. Eluted proteins were diluted with 50 μL of S-Trap buffer (10% SDS in 100 mM Triethyl bicarbonate [TEAB] containing 2 mM dithiothreitol). Following bead removal, the mixture was incubated at 56°C for 30 minutes to reduce disulfide bonds and alkylated for 30 minutes with 4 μL of 62.5 mM iodoacetamide. Protein purification on S-trap micro columns (PROTIFI) were performed following the manufacturers recommendations and digested for 4 hours at 37°C with 2 μg of trypsin. Tryptic peptides were recovered from the S-Trap columns using three consecutive elutions with 40 μL of 50 mM TEAB, 40 μL of 0.2% formic acid (FA) and 40 μL of 50% acetonitrile. 30 μL (~ 20%) of each sample was diluted into pre-equilibrated Evotip Pure chromatography tips containing 180 μL of 0.1% FA, centrifuged at 800 x g for 2 minutes and washed with 200 μL of 0.1% FA prior to LC-MS analysis.

Peptides were separated using a standardized 31-minute gradient “Whisper” method (40SPD) with 0.1% FA and 0.1% FA/99.9% ACN as the mobile phases using an Evosep One liquid chromatography system (Evosep) connected to a 15 cm × 75 μm column packed with 1.9 μm ReproSil-Pur 120 C18-AQ reverse phase beads (Dr. Maisch, Ammerbuch-Entringen, Germany) and introduced into a timsTOF fleX MALDI-2 mass spectrometer (Bruker, Billerica, MA). The data was acquired using a data independent acquisition (DIA) mode with the mass spectrometer executing 12 dia-PASEF MS/MS scans with 2 ion-mobility windows per scan with variable isolation window widths optimized using the py_diAID algorithm (m/z range: 320-1550, mobility range: 0.65-1.5). Each peptide sample was analyzed across duplicate LC-MS runs.

Protein identification and quantification was performed on each individual sample analyzed in DIA mode using DIA-NN (v 1.8.2 beta 8). The search was performed against a dedicated spectral library generated in FragPipe and included the following parameters: variable oxidation of methionine, N-terminus methionine excision and fixed carbamidomethylation of cysteine, with 2 missed tryptic cleavages. Additional parameter ranges were specified: peptide length: 6-40, charge state: 2-6, precursor m/z: 300-1800, fragment ion: 200-1800. Search results were re-annotated using the UniProt database used to build the spectral library. The parameters for the quantitation algorithm were set as follows: mass accuracy: 10 ppm, MS1 accuracy: 15 ppm with match between runs (MBR) enabled, allowed isotopologues, shared spectra exclusion. Gene-based protein inference, double-pass neural network with robust LC quantification and smart profiling were used as additional parameters. Protein abundances were calculated using the iq package (v1.9.12) implemented within the ProteoDA environment and used to calculate the compound-induced blockage relative to the DMSO control. The adjusted p-values associated with each blockage was calculated using the limma package (v3.58.1) implemented within the ProteoDA environment.

For plasmid transfection, 2.5-5 μg of plasmid DNA was incubated at RT with Lipofectamine 3000 transfection reagent (Thermo Fisher) in 0.5 mL Opti-MEM (Fisher Scientific) for 15 min at a 1:2 plasmid-to-Lipofectamine/P3000 ratio and added to cells cultured in a 6-well plate. Media was changed after overnight incubation (approximately 16 hours) and transfection efficiency was assessed after 48 h of incubation.

#### Co-Immunoprecipitation assay

Proteins were immunoprecipitated from RPE-1 whole-cell extracts. Briefly, cells were washed with 1X PBS, collected, and lysed for 30 min on a rotating wheel at 4°C in a buffer containing 20 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.65), 250 mM NaCl, 0.5% NP-40, 5 mM EDTA, 5% glycerol with protease and phosphatase cocktail inhibitors (Roche). Protein concentration was determined by Bradford assay (Thermo Fisher Scientific). 1.5-2 mg of whole-cell extracts were incubated on a rotating wheel for 16-18 hours at 4°C with 3 μg of 53BP1 rabbit antibody (Novus Biological), or an equivalent IgG control (Millipore). Protein A Dynabeads (Invitrogen) were washed 3 times with lysis buffer and incubated with the lysate for 4 hours on a rotating wheel at 4°C. The beads were then washed 5 times with TGN buffer [20 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.65), 150 mM NaCl, 3 mM MgCl2, 10% Glycerol, 0.01% NP-40] for 5 minutes each, followed by elution in 4X SDS loading buffer. Eluted proteins were analyzed by immunoblotting.

#### Statistics and reproducibility

All statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism 10 software unless otherwise specified. p values for RT-qPCR experiments were calculated either by an unpaired t-test or a One-way ANOVA with Dunnett’s multiple comparisons. For immunofluorescence microscopy/PLA, p values were calculated by Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn’s multiple comparisons. All data are representative of 3 independent experiments unless otherwise stated. A p value of p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. In all cases, ns: not significant, p ≥ 0.05; *p < 0.05; **p < 0.01; ***p < 0.001; ****p < 0.0001.

#### Chemical Synthesis General Methods and Materials

All commercially available starting materials were purchased from Sigma Aldrich, Fisher Scientific, Oakwood Chemical, and Combi Blocks. All reagents were used as received without further purification. Anhydrous solvents, such as tetrahydrofuran (THF), dichloromethane (DCM), diethyl ether (Et2O), dimethyl formamide (DMF), dimethylsulfoxide (DMSO), 1,4-dioxane, and toluene were purchased from Fisher Scientific, and used as received. If necessary, air or moisture sensitive reactions were carried out under an inert atmosphere of nitrogen. Removal of solvents was accomplished on a Büchi R-300 rotary evaporator and further concentration was done under a Welch 1400B-01 vacuum line, and/or Labconco FreeZone 6 plus system. Purification of compounds was performed by normal phase column chromatography using Teledyne CombiFlash chromatography system, and/or reversed phase chromatography on Shimadzu LC-20AP chromatography system. The purity was analyzed on Waters Acquity UPLC system. Analytical thin layer chromatography (TLC) plates were purchased from Fisher Scientific (EMD Millipore TLC Silica Gel60 F254). Visualization was accomplished by irradiation under UV light (254 nm).

All 1H-NMR and 13C-NMR spectra were recorded at 298K on a Bruker Ascend 500 (500 MHz) spectrometer. Samples were dissolved in CDCl3 or DMSO-d6 obtained from Cambridge Isotope Laboratories. The spectra were referenced to the residual solvent peak (CDCl3: 7.26 ppm for 1H-NMR and 77.16 ppm for 13C-NMR; DMSO-d6: 2.50 ppm for 1H-NMR and 39.25 ppm for 13C-NMR, CD3OD: 3.31 ppm for 1H NMR and 49.00 ppm for 13C NMR or tetramethylsilane (TMS) as the internal standard. Chemical shift, multiplicity (s=singlet, d=doublet, t=triplet, q=quartet, m=multiplet, br=broad peak), coupling constants (Hz), and number of protons were assigned using MestReNova software. Mass spectrometry (LCMS) data were obtained on Waters Acquity UPLC system in positive ESI mode.

Final compounds submitted for testing were prepared and stored as 10 mM stock solutions in DMSO. Stocks were stored at −20°C and aliquoted as needed for specific experiments to reduce the number of freeze thaw cycles. Unless otherwise noted for specific compounds, no apparent solubility issues were observed with the compounds either in DMSO or aqueous buffer conditions at the concentrations used.
